title: Probiotic neoantigen delivery vectors for precision cancer immunotherapy
source: Redenti et al., show notes for Science TLDR episode 10
one_line: Engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 was rebuilt as an in situ neoantigen vaccine vector that controls or eradicates tumours in mouse colorectal cancer and melanoma models.
key_claims: Removing cryptic plasmids and Lon/OmpT proteases substantially increased neoantigen expression inside the bacteria.
Increasing phagocytosis susceptibility and expressing listeriolysin O improved neoantigen uptake and cytosolic delivery, enabling MHC class I presentation by antigen-presenting cells.
The engineered vaccine elicited potent T cell responses and controlled or eradicated tumours in primary and metastatic models.
Intravenous administration was effective, avoiding the need for direct intratumoural injection.
Systemic anti-tumour immunity cleared distant untreated tumours, and the engineered strain showed reduced blood persistence and minimal side effects versus wild-type E. coli.
limitations: All efficacy data are from mouse models; no human clinical safety or efficacy data.
Neoantigen prediction and selection criteria were not optimised for maximal immunogenicity.
Durability of anti-tumour immunity and recurrence risk were not assessed.
Only colorectal cancer and melanoma models were tested; broader tumour applicability unknown.
Long-term impact on the gut microbiome and scalable clinical manufacturing were not addressed.
open_questions: Do engineered probiotic neoantigen vectors show safety and objective responses in human clinical trials?
Does combination with checkpoint inhibitors or adoptive cell therapy synergise with the vaccine?
How long does the induced systemic immunity persist, and does it prevent recurrence?
Which neoantigen selection algorithm maximises immunogenicity in this delivery format?
